claims.text: PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles supported on SiO2 can be prepared using a one-step colloid-based or solvothermal route.
The one-step colloidal synthesis is performed at 80 °C.
Rapid quenching limits atomic diffusion during formation of PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Limiting atomic diffusion by rapid quenching kinetically traps a homogeneous, single-phase PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy.
Formation of the PtPdCoCuNi HEA produces highly dispersed and isolated Pt and Pd active sites.
A homogeneous single-phase alloy is the reason Pt and Pd remain isolated.
Slow cooling increases atomic mobility in PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
The increased mobility during slow cooling causes local phase segregation.
Phase segregation reduces the isolation of Pt and Pd active sites.
Loss of isolated Pt and Pd sites diminishes catalytic efficiency in nitrobenzene hydrogenation.
Isolated, nucleophilic Pt and Pd sites and their synergistic electronic properties modulate nitrobenzene chemisorption and enhance hydrogenation activity.
DRIFTS can provide evidence for isolated Pt and Pd sites in this PtPdCoCuNi catalyst.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have a more uniform, single-phase structure and greater atomic-level disorder than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will contain more isolated noble-metal sites than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 will give more than twice the nitrobenzene-hydrogenation yield of a slowly cooled sample.
Slowly cooled PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles are expected to exhibit phase segregation and reduced catalytic performance.
The proposed cooling-rate mechanism should apply specifically to SiO2-supported PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles made by the stated low-temperature one-step route with controlled precursor mixing.
